candidate_windows.window_text:
Datasets We evaluated our method on the XSUM (Narayan et al., 2018) dataset. XSUM contains 226,711 online British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) articles covering domains like news, politics, sports, business and more. Each article is paired with a single sentence summary written by the BBC journalists. The dataset is split into three subsets: training (204,045, $90\%$ ), validation (11,332, $5\%$ ), and test (11,334, $5\%$ ) sets. We choose XSUM because it is more abstractive than other summarization datasets. It also relatively noisy due to the way it is created (Maynez et al., 2020).

For fine-grained entity-level factuality analysis (see Section 5.1), we use the XENT dataset created by Cao et al. (2022). XENT contains 800 article and summary pairs where the articles are sampled from XSUM test set and the summaries are generated using a fine-tuned BART model (Lewis et al., 2020). In XENT, each entity in the summary is annotated with three labels: non-hallucinated, factual hallucination, and non-factual hallucination. Factual hallucinations refer to an entity that is verifiable by world knowledge but not directly inferable from the source text. We evaluate our model on the test set of XENT which contains 240 summaries and 835 entities.

Baselines We compare our method with five baselines: (1) State-of-the-art abstractive summarization model BART (Lewis et al., 2020). (2) The loss truncation method proposed by Kang and Hashimoto (2020). (3) The token-level loss truncation method proposed by Goyal et al. (2022). (4) GOLD (generation by off-policy learning from demonstrations), an off-policy RL algorithm proposed by Pang and He (2021). (5) A factuality-aware off-policy RL algorithm for text summarization proposed by (Cao et al., 2022).

BART is a frequently used transformer-based model for summarization. It employs the encoder-decoder architecture, which is essentially a denoising autoencoder that reconstructs the original text with injected noise, such as token deletion, replacement, masking and sentence permutation. The loss truncation method proposed by Kang and Hashimoto (2020) adaptively discards high log loss examples as a way to reduce hallucination in generation. Similarly, the token-level loss truncation in Goyal et al. (2022) removes high-loss and low-loss tokens that are challenging or too easy to learn. GOLD (Pang and He, 2021) is proposed to alleviate the discrepancies between training and evaluation objectives in MLE (e.g., over-generalization, exposure bias). Pang and He (2021) shows that GOLD outperforms BART on text summarization in terms of ROUGE scores and human evaluation. Cao et al. (2022) augmented GOLD with factuality rewards generated using their entity-level factuality classifier.

Implementation Details In the following experiments, we use pre-trained BART-LARGE as the backbone for our model. The size of hidden layers is set to 1024 and the max sequence length is set to 1024 for both the encoder and decoder modules. We fine-tuned our model on the XSUM training set for 20,000 steps with a warm-up period of 500 steps. We use the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, 2014) with $\epsilon = 1\mathrm{e} - 8$ and an initial learning rate 3e-5. Both dropout and attention dropout are applied in each layer with a dropout rate set to 0.1. The $\alpha$ in Equation 3 is set to 1.0 unless otherwise specified. We use the sum regularizer defined in Equation 5 for our main results. All experiments are conducted on 4 Tesla V100 GPUs with 32GB of memory.

Automated Evaluation Metrics For sentence-level faithfulness evaluation, we use FACTCC (Kryscinski et al., 2020) and DAE (Goyal and Durrett, 2021). FACTCC is a sentence-level faithfulness classifier trained on synthetic dataset that is created based on analysis of errors made by state-of-the-art summarization models. DAE is trained on fine-grained, human annotations of factual errors made by abstractive summarization models. Given a document and summary pair $(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ , both methods predict a label $y\in \{0,1\}$ where 0 indicts the summary being non-faithful and 1 being faithful. The percentage of sentences that are predicted

as faithful by the classifier is used as the sentence factuality rate.

For entity-level factuality evaluation, we use ENTFA proposed by Cao et al. (2022). ENTFA is a $k$ -NN model that uses prior and posterior probabilities as features to predict the factuality and hallucination status of the entities in a given summary. We use the percentage of entities in the output summaries that are predicted as non-factual hallucinations as the entity hallucination rate in Table 2. For all three evaluation methods, we use the evaluation scripts and parameters provided in the papers. To measure the impact of each method on summary abstractiveness, we calculate the percentage of novel $n$ -grams and coverage, the percentage of words in the summary that are part of an extractive fragment of the source document (Grusky et al., 2018)
